cases.quote: The following are lists of (non-ideographic) characters from a subset of ISO/IEC 10646 (collection number 285 "BASIC JAPANESE" and 286 "JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHICS EXTENSION") grouped by character class according to the classification explained in § 3.9.2 Grouping of Characters and Symbols depending on their Positioning.
cases.rationale: A.6's first row is U+3002 IDEOGRAPHIC FULL STOP, common name 句点, with an empty Remarks cell, and Appendix A's preamble binds that table to cl-06. U+3002 is listed by A.6 and by no other table anywhere in Appendix A, so nothing the caller declares can move it: the key alone decides the class, and an implementation may answer without consulting the frame, the role or the neighbors. The caller declares the half em because that is the character advance § 3.1.2 states for cl-06 ('The character advance of commas (cl-07), full stops (cl-06), opening brackets (cl-01), closing brackets (cl-02) and middle dots (cl-05) is half-width (half em)'), so this is the occurrence supplied by a caller who set the glyph on JLReq's own geometry. The case declares no direction because A.6's first row states no restriction: § 3.1.1 makes U+3002 the cl-06 member of vertical writing mode and of two of its three horizontal conventions.

permitted.source: JLReq A.6 row 1 (U+3002), under the A preamble

cases.quote: The character advance of commas (cl-07), full stops (cl-06), opening brackets (cl-01), closing brackets (cl-02) and middle dots (cl-05) is half-width (half em). But when those punctuation marks are placed side-by-side with ideographic (cl-19), hiragana (cl-15), or katakana (cl-16) characters, in principle, a given amount of spacing will be inserted before or after the symbols, which makes them appear as if they were intrinsically full-width (one em).
cases.rationale: The same key on the other frame: the advance a modern OpenType font reports for 。 is a full em, because the conditional space § 3.1.2 describes is already inside it. The expected class is byte-identical to the case above, and that equality is the assertion. A.6 states no frame for U+3002 at all — its Remarks cell is empty — so the frame here decides a geometry and never a class, which is the distinction ADR 0008 turns on. An implementation that reads the frame as a class selector, or that refuses a cl-06 occurrence whose advance is not half an em, differs from the document here; an implementation that answers 6 from the key alone agrees with both cases and has to do no work.

permitted.source: JLReq A.6 row 1 (U+3002), with the frame of § 3.1.2

cases.quote: To work around this issue, many existing implementations use compatibility characters encoded separately in the standard for the purpose of round-trip integrity with the legacy encoding standards. For example, while this document lists U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS as a member of opening brackets (cl-01), the compatibility counterpart U+FF08 FULLWIDTH LEFT PARENTHESIS is used in the Japanese context in most Japanese text layout software.
cases.rationale: The text is U+FF0E FULLWIDTH FULL STOP, which is the glyph A.6's own Character (字形) column prints in its second row while that row's UCS column reads 002E and its Name column reads FULL STOP. The Character column is an illustration and not the key: the same key 002E is illustrated as an ASCII period in A.24 and in A.27. One code point, two illustrations, one key. Appendix A's preamble Note, quoted above, states the convention for the whole appendix, so a caller who supplies U+FF0E has supplied A.6's second key on the full-width frame that code point itself asserts, and that frame is also what leaves cl-06 alone standing: A.24 covers 'European numerals which are not full-width' and states 'quarter em width or half-width' in its Remarks, and A.27 states 'proportionally-spaced'. An implementation that keys Appendix A by the printed glyph, or that folds nothing, finds no table row for U+FF0E and reports no class for the commonest way a Japanese full stop is actually encoded in horizontal text.

permitted.source: JLReq A.6 row 2 (U+002E) reached through the A preamble Note

cases.quote: In horizontal writing mode, there are three conventions in choice of symbols for full stops (cl-06) and commas (cl-07): 1. Using COMMA "，" and FULL STOP "．" (see Figure 57). 2. Using COMMA "，" and IDEOGRAPHIC FULL STOP "。" (see Figure 58). 3. Using IDEOGRAPHIC COMMA "、" and IDEOGRAPHIC FULL STOP "。" (see Figure 59).
cases.rationale: A.6's second and last row is U+002E FULL STOP, common name ピリオド, and it is the only row in the class carrying a Remark: 'used in horizontal composition' / '横組で使用'. § 3.1.1 unpacks that Remark into the rule the two words only gesture at, and the case declares the direction the Remark names. The period is set on the half em because that is the advance § 3.1.2 states for cl-06, and that declaration is the whole difference between this case and the one below it. Two other Appendix A tables list this same key and neither reaches this occurrence: A.27's Remarks cell reads 'proportionally-spaced', which the caller has not declared, and cl-24 is 'characters in a grouped numeral' (連数字中の文字), whose § 3.9.2 description is 'the decimal point or the comma and space used as a decimal place indicator in numbers' — a period between two hiragana is in no numeral, so its membership cannot arise. Membership of cl-24 is a property of the construct the occurrence sits in, and this occurrence sits in none.

permitted.source: JLReq A.6 row 2 (U+002E), Remarks 'used in horizontal composition'

forbidden.why: A.27 lists U+002E with the Remark 'proportionally-spaced', and this occurrence declares the half em § 3.1.2 states for cl-06. Answering cl-27 for every ASCII period reads the code point and ignores the frame, which is the axis Appendix A's Remarks column uses to separate the two.

cases.quote: The usage of these two differently designed commas should be explicit. Usually, in a Japanese context Japanese design is used, and in Western context Western design is used. However, there are some ambiguous cases, such as "エディター（editor）は……". In this case, English spelling is indicated using parentheses in a Japanese line of text. In this particular case, Japanese design is better.
cases.rationale: This is where cl-06 stops. The input is byte-identical to the case above except for the period's declared frame and the advance that frame describes, and the class changes: A.27's Remarks cell for U+002E reads 'proportionally-spaced', § 3.1.2 states the character advance of cl-06 is half-width, and no frame satisfies both, so the same code point in the same neighborhood is a Western character (cl-27) when the caller set the Western design and a full stop (cl-06) when they set the Japanese one. The § 3.9.2 Note quoted above is the document's own account of that pair, and it concedes an ambiguity — but the concession is about which design an author should choose, not about how a described occurrence is classified: the same Note requires the usage to be explicit, and the declared frame is that explicitness. So this case has one answer rather than two. A case pinning the concession itself would have to name an occurrence whose design is undeclared, and this format has no such occurrence, because an item whose key A.6 names must declare a frame.

forbidden.why: § 3.1.2 states the character advance of full stops (cl-06) is half-width, and A.27 states this key is proportionally-spaced. An occurrence measured on the proportional frame is not a cl-06 occurrence, whatever its neighbors are.

cases.quote: Sequences of European numerals which are not full-width and are handled as Japanese text, the decimal point or the comma and space used as a decimal place indicator in numbers.
cases.rationale: The second boundary of the class, and the one the frame cannot draw. A.24 lists the same key U+002E that A.6 lists, with the Remarks 'decimal point / quarter em width or half-width', and A.6 states no frame for it at all, so half-width is a frame both classes accept: an implementation separating cl-06 from cl-24 by the advance alone has nothing to separate them with. What separates them is the job the document gives the occurrence, which § 3.9.2's description of cl-24 states — the decimal point in a number — and which this case declares as the decimal-point role on a period between two European numerals. The two neighboring digits are not what this case asks about; they are what makes the role true.

forbidden.why: The answer an implementation gives that decides cl-06 from the key and the half-width frame. Both are equally true of A.24's row for the same key, so neither excludes it; § 3.9.2 gives the decimal point to grouped numerals (cl-24), and this occurrence declares that role.

cases.quote: A few character classes of this document are modified from JIS X 4051. In § A. Character Classes, there is a whole mapping table to ISO/IEC 10646 Annex A collection 285 (BASIC JAPANESE) and collection 286 (JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHIC EXTENSION). All character classes of this document are as follows:
cases.rationale: The third boundary, and the one a reader rather than a font gets wrong. A question mark ends a Japanese sentence exactly as a full stop does, and the document puts it elsewhere: § 3.9.2's list gives cl-04 dividing punctuation marks (区切り約物) the examples ！？ and gives cl-06 the examples 。．, and A.4 enumerates U+0021, U+003F, U+203C, U+2047, U+2048 and U+2049 while A.6 enumerates U+3002 and U+002E and stops. The distinction is not cosmetic: § 3.1.2 makes a cl-06 advance half-width while § 3.1.6 sets dividing punctuation marks on the full-width frame and puts a full em after a sentence-final one, so an implementation that classifies by 'this terminates a sentence' produces half an em of error at every question mark. The input is U+FF1F, the compatibility counterpart of the A.4 key U+003F, on the full-width frame that code point asserts — which is also what excludes A.27's proportionally-spaced listing of the same key.

forbidden.why: A.6 enumerates two keys, U+3002 and U+002E, and neither is U+003F. § 3.9.2 lists ！？ under dividing punctuation marks (cl-04) and 。．under full stops (cl-06), with no 'etc.' on the second.

cases.quote: As noted in § B. Spacing between Characters and § C.2 Notes , there are several conventions for line-start prohibition, line-end prohibition and unbreakable character rules. The following lists four levels of convention. Note that breaking a line after opening brackets (cl-01) and before closing brackets (cl-02), full stops (cl-06) or commas (cl-07) is prohibited at all levels. Likewise, those rules common to all levels are not listed below.
cases.rationale: § C.3 publishes four conventions for line-start prohibition (行頭禁則) and lets a caller choose between them, and the sentence quoted above takes the boundary before a full stop out of that choice: it is prohibited at every level, so no setting of kinsoku.level changes this answer. That is what the four permitted entries below record — one per choice, all with the same expectation — and recording it as four entries rather than as one is deliberate, because the assertion is about the selector rather than about a single setting. The caller's own line breaker offers a break at this boundary, which is why the candidate is declared: an implementation that honors UAX #14 here puts 。 at a line head, and the sentence above says no convention permits that. § 3.1.7 states the same fact from the line-head side, in the same words the four levels are written against.

permitted.source: JLReq § C.3, the sentence common to all four levels
JLReq § C.3 level 1 (very loose), which does not list this boundary
JLReq § C.3 level 2 (loose), which does not list this boundary
JLReq § C.3 level 3 (strict), which does not list this boundary
JLReq § C.3 level 4 (very strict), which does not list this boundary

forbidden.why: § C.3: 'breaking a line ... before closing brackets (cl-02), full stops (cl-06) or commas (cl-07) is prohibited at all levels'. The Japanese half states the same exemption from the level selector, so no reading of the section makes this boundary breakable.
